Village Craft Guide

Five Krownlandia village traditions and a Sewing Club exercise to explore without the 3D park. Try the paper exercises in any order, or describe your designs aloud. They award no points and do not change your park progress.

  • Riverbend: pottery and baskets
  • Riverbend: watch an imagined float
  • Eldergrove: wooden plaques
  • Stonehearth: stone patterns
  • Meadowbrook: weaving
  • Meadowbrook: market table
  • Whispering Pines: pinewood inlay
  • Sewing Club: stitch sampler

Riverbend: pottery and baskets

The recorded Riverbend village description includes pottery and woven baskets (page 3). In the park, Discover Riverbend offers both practices.

Try it on paper: Outline a bowl or a vase. Give it a repeating band of dots or waves. For a basket instead, number four bands from bottom to top, choose light or dark for each, and add a low or arched handle.

Riverbend: watch an imagined float

The recorded Riverbend village description mentions fishing (page 3). This is a paper or spoken companion to the prototype’s optional riverside cast. You don’t need gear, and there is no catch, timer, score or saved progress.

  1. Imagine the bank on one side and moving water farther out. Choose where to put an imaginary float.
  2. Near the bank: Imagine the float resting beside the shore. When you reel it in, picture or describe the ring it leaves.
  3. In the current: Imagine the float drifting along. When you reel it in, draw or describe the curved wake it leaves on its way back.

Try both spots. How would you tell a friend which float moved before you reeled it in? In the park, open Discover Riverbend → Try a riverside cast for the button version.

Eldergrove: wooden plaques

The recorded Eldergrove description includes woodcraft. In the park, the woodcraft shelter offers Woodcraft practice.

Try it on paper: Choose an oval or square plaque. Place a leaf or branch motif inside it. Describe the shape and motif so someone could imagine your design without seeing it.

Stonehearth: stone patterns

The recorded Stonehearth description includes stone architecture and masonry. Its courtyard offers Arrange a stone pattern.

Try it on paper: Make a two-by-two grid. Label each tile smooth or striped. Say the four choices in reading order: top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right.

Meadowbrook: weaving

The recorded Meadowbrook description includes textiles, natural dyes, and weaving (page 2). Search the park map for Meadowbrook weaving table if you want to try the in-park sampler.

Try it on paper: Draw six rows. Choose rose or gold for each row, or write the color names instead. Try a repeating sequence, then change one row and describe what changed.

Meadowbrook: market table

The recorded Meadowbrook village description includes produce markets (page 2). These produce choices and the basket exercise come from the prototype, not a historical vendor list.

Try it on paper or aloud: Give three empty baskets the labels first, second, and third. For each basket, choose Apples, Carrots, or Leafy greens. You can repeat a choice. Read the finished table in order so somebody else could recreate it without seeing it.

Try a variation: Change only the middle basket. Tell a partner which basket changed and which two stayed the same. Then try a table with the same produce at both ends and a different choice in the middle.

In the park, search the Park map for Meadowbrook market table to try this at the worktable. It is practice only; nothing is bought, traded, scored, or saved.

Whispering Pines: pinewood inlay

The recorded village description includes woodworking and resin crafts. In the park, the story board and bench offer Pinewood inlay practice.

Try it on paper: Draw three slots labeled left, center, and right. Pick pinewood or amber for each. Try matching the outer slots and using the other material in the center. This is a design exercise with imaginary materials.

Sewing Club: stitch sampler

The original inventory lists Sewing Club, credited to @lisachandler (page 16). In the park, the Clubhouse board offers a practice sampler. This version uses the same pattern and needs no sewing tools.

Try it on paper or aloud: Imagine six spaces in a row. In each space, say or write the stitch length, or draw a line of that length. Work from left to right.

Practice pattern: Short, Long, Short, Short, Long, Short.

Read the row back. Which two spaces have long stitches? Now turn the row around. Do the lengths change? Try a second row with just one length changed. Describe the difference by giving its position and new length.

The recorded village descriptions are the inspiration. The workshop layouts, choices, and paper exercises are interpretations made for this prototype.
